summary: This paper demonstrates strong ZZ coupling between capacitively coupled transmon qubits, achieving cross-Kerr interaction strengths up to 350 MHz—more than an order of magnitude larger than prior capacitive implementations—and uses this to observe a dynamical blockade effect analogous to Rydberg-atom dipole blockade. The engineered longitudinal interaction enables interaction-dominated physics in superconducting circuits suitable for globally controlled quantum architectures.
motivation: Rydberg atoms achieve strong collective phenomena through large state-dependent interactions, but superconducting qubits typically have weak intrinsic ZZ coupling. The authors sought to engineer strong longitudinal interactions purely through capacitive coupling to realize blockade-mediated physics and globally controlled quantum operations without increasing control line complexity.
method: Two transmon qubits were fabricated with direct capacitive coupling ($C_{12} = 5.11$ fF). The ZZ interaction strength $\zeta(\Delta)$ was characterized via two-tone spectroscopy and Ramsey interferometry as a function of qubit detuning $\Delta$, and blockade was demonstrated by applying sequential $\pi$-pulses with variable delay. Black-box circuit quantization and Schrieffer–Wolff perturbation theory explained the results.
result: The measured $\zeta$ ranged from $10$ MHz at $\Delta/(2\pi) = 2$ GHz to $350$ MHz near resonance, scaling as $\propto J^2/\Delta$ where $J/(2\pi) \approx 240$ MHz. Blockade was observed: exciting Q2 first suppressed Q1 excitation with $\zeta/(2\pi) = 19$ MHz, with suppression lifting on the $T_1$ timescale of Q2 ($\sim 8$ μs for chip 1). Results validated on a second device with X-mon geometry and comparable coherence ($T_1 \sim 15$ μs, $T_2^{\mathrm{echo}} \sim 20$ μs).
